query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated predictive model that combines machine‐learned interatomic potentials with coupled Boltzmann transport calculations—treating anharmonic phonon scattering and electron‐phonon interactions independently while accounting for realistic defect and 1 wt.% oxygen effects—will separately and accurately predict the lattice and electronic contributions to heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr. Compared to previous approaches that conflate these mechanisms or rely on oversimplified Debye models, this method is expected to improve the overall predictive accuracy by roughly 20% over the temperature range where each mechanism dominates.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk crystalline HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy containing a realistic distribution of defects and 1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
generation.intervention: Application of a new computational approach that integrates machine learning interatomic potentials with coupled Boltzmann transport calculations in order to explicitly and separately model anharmonic phonon (lattice) scattering and electron‐phonon interactions (electronic conduction).
generation.conditions: Temperature regimes ranging from below 200 K (where experimental evidence indicates that lattice and electronic contributions are nearly comparable) to 300–1200 K (where oxygen impurities impact the overall conductivity, with total values reported between 10–17 W/(K m)).
generation.structural_mediator: Realistic atomic-scale defect distributions and oxygen-induced local lattice distortions in the bulk high-entropy alloy structure, which mediate separate conduction channels for phonons and electrons.
generation.mechanism: By accurately capturing the atomic-scale complexity including anharmonic phonon scattering and electron-phonon coupling separately—not relying on a single Debye temperature or ideal defect-free approximations—the model will yield independent predictions for lattice and electronic thermal conductivities. This separation allows for direct comparison with experiments that resolve the two contributions under different thermal regimes.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict nearly equal lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K and a distinct trend at higher temperatures (300–1200 K) that matches total conductivity measurements of 10–17 W/(K m). The overall predictive accuracy (in terms of quantitative agreement with experimental data) is expected to be improved by about 20% compared to earlier analytical models.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical approaches and simulations that either conflate lattice and electronic transport or rely on Debye temperature based models assuming perfect, defect-free crystals.
generation.boundary: Applicable to well-characterized bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens with controlled oxygen levels over the temperature range from under 200 K (where both contributions are comparable) to about 1200 K (where oxygen effects become significant). Predictions may become less reliable if the defect distribution deviates strongly from that assumed in the model or outside this temperature window.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the 20% improvement is an approximate estimate; sensitivity to the precise defect/impurity distributions and potential unmodeled scattering mechanisms may introduce additional uncertainties in the predicted separation of conduction contributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize high-quality HfNbTaTiZr samples with a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen content and a realistic defect distribution. Perform thermal conductivity measurements over the temperature range below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K. Use experimental techniques (e.g., combining direct thermal conductivity measurements with electrical conductivity and the Wiedemann-Franz law) to independently extract lattice and electronic contributions.
measurements: Total thermal conductivity across the temperature range.
Independent estimates of the lattice (phononic) and electronic contributions (using techniques such as differential measurements under magnetic fields to suppress electronic conduction).
Comparison of the measured contributions with the separate predictions from the new model.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental separation of lattice and electronic contributions fails to show the predicted trends (e.g., nearly equal contributions below 200 K and a total conductivity in the range 10–17 W/(K m) at 300–1200 K) or if the overall prediction error is not reduced by approximately 20% compared to previous models, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

decision.trend: Early efforts modeled heat transport in high-entropy alloys by varying atomic masses and force constants or by coupling DFT-derived elastic properties with simple analytical (often Debye-based) conductivity estimates. These approaches typically assumed perfect, defect‐free crystals and did not differentiate between lattice (phononic) and electronic carriers, even though experiments suggest that both contributions can be comparable (especially below 200 K) and that impurities (e.g., 1 wt.% oxygen) play a significant role at higher temperatures.
decision.unsolved: Existing methods do not account for the full atomic‐scale complexity of HfNbTaTiZr, particularly regarding the independent quantification of lattice and electronic contributions, the influence of realistic defect/impurity distributions, and the challenging temperature-dependent interplay of these transport mechanisms.
decision.lever: Integrate machine learning interatomic potentials with coupled Boltzmann transport calculations that explicitly treat anharmonic phonon scattering (for lattice conduction) and electron‐phonon interactions (for electronic conduction), while incorporating realistic defect and impurity effects (especially oxygen).
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the trend by moving beyond oversimplified Debye models and ideal crystal assumptions, thereby capturing the true atomic-scale complexity. It would separately predict lattice and electronic contributions across the 200–1200 K temperature range. The model is expected to improve predictive accuracy by approximately 20% over earlier methods as indicated by tighter agreement with distinct low‐temperature (where contributions are comparable) and high‐temperature oxygen-impacted experimental measurements.
